title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1.III: not Augustine alone — Milevis can. 4, African exiles, Orange can. 4 preach creating/vivifying grace that works both to will and to do
pass_a_gloss: But someone will say, This was Augustine’s singular sentence, into which the opinion of absolute predestination drew him. Nay, it was common unto all the Orthodox, as is plain from the Councils celebrated against Pelagius and the Semipelagians. From the Milevitan, canon 4, By the grace of Christ it is granted unto us that what we have known ought to be done, we also love and are able to do. A little after, Both are God’s gift, both to know what we ought to do, and to love that we may do. From the Synodical Epistle of the African Bishops exiled in Sardinia the same is plain: God commands a man that he will, but the Lord works in the man also to will: he commands that he do, but works also to do. God in quickening men waits for no beginning of the human will, but quickens by making the good will itself. Finally from the Council of Orange the same is clear; canon 4, If anyone contends that God waits for our will that we may be purged from sin, and does not confess that even our willing to be purged is wrought in us by the infusion and operation of the Holy Spirit, he resists the Holy Spirit himself speaking through Solomon, The will is prepared by the Lord, and the Apostle wholesomely preaching, It is God who works in us both to will and to finish according to his good will.
pass_b_english: Someone will say this was Augustine’s private view, pulled in by absolute predestination. No: it was common to all the Orthodox, as the anti-Pelagian councils show. Milevis canon 4: By Christ’s grace it is granted us that what we know ought to be done, we also love and can do. A little later: Both are God’s gift—to know what we ought to do, and to love so that we do. The synodical letter of the African bishops exiled in Sardinia is the same: God commands a man to will, but the Lord works in the man also to will; he commands to do, but works also to do. In quickening men God waits for no start of the human will; he quickens by making the good will itself. Orange canon 4 is clear: If anyone contends God waits for our will so we may be purged from sin, and does not confess that even our willing to be purged is wrought in us by the Spirit’s infusion and working, he resists the Holy Spirit speaking through Solomon, The will is prepared by the Lord, and the Apostle, It is God who works in us both to will and to finish according to his good will.
source_text: Sed dixerit aliquis, Haec fuit singularis Augustini sententia, in quam absolutae praedestinationis opinio eum pertraxit. Imo fuit omnium Orthodoxorum communis, ut ex Conciliis contra Pelagium et Semipelagianos celebratis constat. Ex Milevitano, canone 4, Per gratiam Christi nobis praestatur, ut quod faciendum cognoverimus, etiam facere diligamus atque valeamus. Paulo post, Utrumque donum Dei est, et scire quid facere debeamus, et diligere ut faciamus. Ex Epistola Synodica Episcoporum Africanorum in Sardinia exsulum idem patet: Jubet Deus homini ut velit, sed Dominus in homine operatur et velle: jubet ut faciat, sed operatur et facere. Deus in vivificandis hominibus nullum initium humanae voluntatis exspectat, sed ipsam voluntatem bonam faciendo vivificat. Demum ex Concilio Arausicano idem liquet; canone 4, Si quis, ut a peccato purgemur, voluntatem nostram Deum exspectare contendit, non autem ut etiam purgari velimus per Sancti Spiritus infusionem et operationem in nos fieri confitetur, resistit ipsi Spiritui Sancto per Solomonem dicenti, Praeparatur voluntas a Domino, et Apostolo salubriter praedicanti, Deus est qui operatur in nobis et velle et perficere pro bona sua voluntate.
